title: Outbound stability guidelines and IP stickiness (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This note captures guidelines and a pragmatic upgrade/migration plan for improving outbound IP stability and internal private DNS behavior in Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). The primary goal is to reduce downstream friction for customer integrations that require stable source IPs or predictable DNS resolution, while preserving robust scaling and failover properties for Redwood private clusters. This is a working doc — technical decisions, Terraform snippets, and rollout steps are intentionally prescriptive but marked with open questions where we need engineering sign-off.

Background and motivation:
- Several customers have hit failures when their firewall allowlists or partner endpoints require static client IPs. Our current preference for ephemeral NAT addresses (for autoscaled pools) reduces cost but increases churn in outbound source IP addresses.
- Private DNS has been mostly split-horizon but some environments show latency spikes when internal resolvers are overloaded or when NAT path changes cause asymmetric routing.
- We need a repeatable upgrade path (Terraform-first) so existing on-prem/VPC customers can opt into higher IP stability SLAs without heavy manual ops.

Constraints and non-goals:
- Non-goal: Permanently solve every third-party firewall policy (those customers should still use customer-managed egress appliances where required).
- Constraint: Minimal changes to control plane; majority of changes should be infra/config (Terraform modules + curated defaults).
- Constraint: Preserve autoscaling/burst behavior; do not prevent burst capacity during traffic spikes.

Design principles:
1. Explicit intent: defaults should prefer cost-efficient ephemeral NAT pools; stable IPs must be opt-in per-tenant or per-environment.
2. Layered approach: provide (a) sticky SNAT allocation for session affinity, (b) reserved static NAT option for allowlist needs, and (c) DNS sharding + TTL guidance to reduce resolver load.
3. Terraform-first: any changeable knob should be exposed via terraform variables and documented in the private-deployments module set.
4. Observability: instrument NAT exhaustion, IP churn, DNS resolution latency; surfaced in Redwood Console dashboards per-customer.

Recommended architecture (summary):
- Outbound NAT layer: keep autoscaled NAT pool for most traffic. Add a "sticky allocator" service that pins flows from a given instance (or pod IP range) to a stable egress IP for the session lifetime (configurable, default 30m).
- Reserved IP pools: allow customers to allocate 1-5 reserved public IPs (or customer-provided egress IPs for on-prem) via terraform variable enable_reserved_ips = true. Routing policy pins their high-value flows to reserved pool via route tables or policy-based NAT.
- DNS: implement lightweight DNS sharding for internal resolvers: split keys by availability zone / subnet and use short default TTLs for internal records with optional sticky caching on per-cluster DNS forwarders.

Terraform module notes (implementation guidance):
- Module: private-deployments/nat (new module or extension)
  - Inputs (variables):
    - enable_reserved_ips (bool) default = false
    - reserved_ip_count (number) default = 0
    - sticky_session_minutes (number) default = 30
    - nat_pool_min_size (number) default = 2
    - nat_pool_max_size (number) default = 50
    - ip_health_check_interval_seconds (number) default = 10
    - dns_shard_ttl_seconds (number) default = 60
  - Outputs:
    - reserved_ips (list)
    - sticky_allocator_endpoint (string)
  - Notes: expose a flag to prefer reserved_ips for specific subnets via map(subnet=>prefer_reserved) so customers can route traffic per-application.

- Example HCL (consumer usage):
  module "rwi_nat" {
    source = "github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules//private/nat"
    enable_reserved_ips = true
    reserved_ip_count = 2
    sticky_session_minutes = 60
    nat_pool_min_size = 4
    nat_pool_max_size = 20
  }

Edge-cases and behaviors to define:
- IP churn vs scaling: sticky allocator should maintain 1:1 mapping between source pod IP and egress IP while session active, but return mapping to pool after idle timeout. This prevents long-term IP leakage while still giving short-term stability.
- Cross-AZ failover: if an AZ becomes unhealthy, sticky mappings bound to that AZ should failover to healthy AZs and we must notify customer via Console that source IP changed (audit event).
- On-prem: we assume customer can route reserved IPs into their perimeter network; provide documentation for NA to coordinate.

Upgrade plan (safe path / terraform-driven):
1) Feature branch: implement module changes and unit tests in terraform-modules repo. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules/pull/312)
2) Canary: enable enable_reserved_ips=false and sticky_session_minutes=30 on a single internal staging deployment. Monitor NAT metrics for 72h.
3) Controlled customer pilot: invite 2 customers (one VPC, one on-prem) to opt-in via a support request ticket (INF-2147). Use reserved_ip_count=2 for pilot.
4) Iterate: address issues from pilot (routing asymmetry, latency, broken DNS lookups).
5) Org-wide opt-in: provide migration playbook + terraform variable sets; default remains cost-efficient ephemeral mode.

Rollback strategy:
- Changes are largely feature-gated via terraform flags. Rollback is: terraform apply with previous module version + enable_reserved_ips=false + ensure sticky_session_minutes=0. For cases where NAT mappings persist for a short TTL, document expected convergence (30-60m).

Testing and verification checklist:
- Functional tests:
  - Verify flow pinning: start a long-lived test flow and assert repeated connections show same source IP for duration of sticky_session_minutes.
  - Verify reserved IP route: traffic from tagged namespace goes out a reserved IP.
  - DNS shard validation: queries to internal service return per-AZ sharded answers and TTL respected.
- Load tests:
  - Ramp per-cluster to nat_pool_max_size and validate no SNAT exhaustion errors.
  - Burst test: sudden 10x increase in short-lived requests to validate autoscale + sticky allocator behavior.
- Failure tests:
  - AZ failover: simulate AZ loss and verify mapping failover and audit notices.
  - NAT gateway reboot: ensure sessions terminate gracefully and that expected IP churn matches configured timeouts.

Monitoring and alerts (proposed thresholds):
- SNAT exhaustion rate > 0.1% of flows in a 5m window -> P1 pager to infra oncall.
- IP churn (unique egress IPs used per hour normalized by baseline) > +200% -> warn -> investigate allocation logic.
- Internal DNS latency p95 > 200ms for 5m -> page SRE.
- Reserved IP utilization < 10% for 7 days -> recommend reducing reserved count or moving flows to ephemeral pool.

Operational runbook (quick steps for operators):
- To enable reserved IPs for a tenant: update terraform var enable_reserved_ips = true + reserved_ip_count = N, then terraform apply. Update route table tags to include tenant id.
- To force rebind of a sticky mapping: call the sticky-allocator API with a "rebind" flag for target pod IP (use sparingly).
- To drain reserved IPs before releasing: mark reserved pool as draining in Console -> Wait for connections to drop below threshold -> terraform apply to reduce reserved_ip_count.

Open questions / discussion items:
- Cost model: how much to charge for reserved IPs/billed per hour vs monthly? Need finance input. (action: @Priya Menon to propose pricing SKU).
- Compliance: customers that require dedicated egress appliances may still prefer full on-prem NAT boxes. We should document differences and recommended plans.
- Sticky allocator placement: should this be an internal sidecar in the control plane, or a separate HA service? Tradeoffs: sidecar gives locality, separate service centralizes state.

Next steps and owners:
- Marco Liu: finalize terraform module interface and open implementation PR (target: PR #312 follow-ups).
- Priya Menon: draft pricing proposal for reserved IPs (due 2024-12-05).
- Evan Strauss: implement Console metrics and reserve IP UI hooks (due 2025-01-15).
- Sofia Alvarez: coordinate pilot customers and create pilot runbook (due 2024-12-20).

Appendix A — Sample observability queries:
- NAT exhausted flows (Cloud provider example): count_over_time(sum by(pod) (nat_errors_total{type="SNAT_EXHAUSTION"})[5m])
- Sticky allocator mapping count: avg(sticky_mappings_active) by (cluster)

Appendix B — Known limitations:
- On some clouds, reserved IPs add cost and introduce additional route table complexity (we document provider-specific steps in the Terraform README).
- DNS sharding requires forwarder capacity planning — too many shards can increase management overhead.

Document history:
- 2024-11-10: initial draft (Marco)
- 2024-11-21: added Terraform variable matrix and sticky allocator behavior (Evan)
- 2024-12-02: pilot plan and monitoring thresholds updated (Sofia)
- 2025-01-08: minor edits and linked PR + tickets added

Notes-to-self: leave explicit examples of iptables/pbr rules for on-prem customers in a separate follow-up doc. Also collect customer feedback examples during pilot and escalate any partner API limitations.
